segments.title: Turning non-laboratory evidence into analytical writing
segments.summary: The advanced methods lesson connects research design to paragraph structure and warns that evidence earns little unless the writer analyzes it and links it into a coherent argument.
segments.body: The lesson begins with the relationship between gathering evidence and presenting an argument. COVID-19 restrictions had closed laboratory access, so the discussion turns to methods that students could still use. The statement-evidence-analysis-link structure shows why a large body of research does not speak for itself. Marks depend on explaining what the evidence means and connecting each paragraph to the larger claim. Weak analysis in the final write-up can squander extensive earlier work.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke introduces non-laboratory research and explains why evidence must be analyzed and linked rather than merely listed.

segments.title: Literature studies, systematic reviews, and primary research
segments.summary: Different departments may label a literature study as a systematic, systemic, thematic, or prior-research review, but the dissertation still needs enough evidence and a defensible contribution of primary research.
segments.body: Departments use several overlapping names for evidence-led reviews, and students should concentrate on the required work rather than become distracted by terminology. At bachelor's and master's level, the central task is to assemble a substantial evidence base and identify what counts as the project's primary or original research. Losing access to a laboratory changes the available methods without removing the need for a defensible research contribution. Master's work differs chiefly in the expected depth of critical analysis and the larger word count available for it.

evidence.note: The lecture compares names for literature-led reviews, discusses primary research, and distinguishes bachelor’s from master’s work by analytical depth.

segments.title: Combining literature, case studies, interviews, and surveys
segments.summary: Several viable dissertation designs combine a literature study with case studies, interviews, or surveys, using interviews for qualitative depth and surveys for larger quantities of comparable data.
segments.body: Projects without laboratory access can combine several methods according to the question and the researcher's strengths. A literature study supplies context and maps the existing debate, while case studies bring evidence together around particular events, objects, or problems. Interviews provide original qualitative material through detailed answers. Surveys can produce much larger quantities of quantitative data for charts and comparisons. The useful design is the combination that produces enough evidence while remaining practical for the researcher.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke compares combinations of literature studies, case studies, interviews, and surveys, including qualitative and quantitative outputs.

segments.title: A naval historian's dissertation method in practice
segments.summary: One naval-history dissertation relied wholly on archives, while another combined interviews with tightly focused case studies of amphibious operations in a particular war.
segments.body: These examples make the method choices concrete. One dissertation depended entirely on archival research. Another combined a literature study, interviews, and detailed case studies of amphibious operations within a war. The case studies narrowed a large conflict into specific events that could be examined in depth without losing the broader historical setting. This historical and social-science approach also offers science or engineering students an alternative when laboratory access is limited.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke describes his archival dissertation and a naval-history project built around interviews and amphibious-operation case studies.

segments.title: Building a balanced literature study across source types
segments.summary: A literature study can be organized by research objectives while deliberately alternating journal articles, books, and magazines, then giving each source more analytical space than a conventional literature review.
segments.body: A literature study should mix journal articles, books, and magazines rather than allow one format to dominate. Grouping the material under the dissertation's objectives or subtopics keeps each discussion tied to the central question. A conventional literature review may devote one or two paragraphs to a work, while the expanded study uses at least three analytical paragraphs. The extra space supports deeper analysis rather than a longer summary. This structure turns broad reading into an ordered critical chapter.

evidence.note: The lecture recommends mixing source types, grouping them by dissertation objectives, and expanding each source discussion beyond a standard literature review.

segments.title: Testing provenance, results, and conclusions
segments.summary: A three-part source assessment asks who produced and funded the work, what the evidence actually shows, and how much value the source has for the dissertation’s wider argument.
segments.body: The first analytical paragraph establishes where, when, why, and by whom the research was conducted. Work produced by a government, university, commercial company, or opaquely funded think tank may carry different incentives or limitations. The second paragraph compares the reported results with the claims made in the conclusion, since confident conclusions can outrun the data. The third assesses the source from the perspective of the whole dissertation rather than one narrow objective. Together, these tests examine provenance, internal consistency, and relevance.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke sets out three analytical paragraphs covering provenance and funding, findings versus claims, and value to the wider dissertation.

segments.title: Academic voice and the tradeoffs of a fixed word count
segments.summary: Critical judgment can be expressed in impersonal academic language, while every extra paragraph must justify the space it takes from another part of a dissertation’s fixed word count.
segments.body: The lesson recommends expressing academic judgment without first-person phrases such as "I think." Wording such as "the balance of evidence would suggest" states a reasoned position while keeping the emphasis on the argument. Synthesis paragraphs may tie a group of works together after the individual analyses. The dissertation's word count is finite, so extra analysis in the literature study reduces the space available elsewhere. Every additional paragraph has to justify the attention it takes from another part of the project.

evidence.note: The lecture discusses impersonal academic phrasing, section synthesis, and balancing analytical depth against a fixed word count.

segments.title: Choosing viable case studies and recording every source
segments.summary: A useful case study must be relevant, well documented, and realistically accessible. Complete source records protect a deeply immersed researcher from accidental plagiarism.
segments.body: Case selection starts with relevance to the research question, although relevance alone is insufficient. Enough material must exist, and the researcher must be able to reach it under real constraints such as closed archives, travel restrictions, and interview access. Comparative projects should use at least three cases, preferably four, provided each remains viable. Intensive study can make a researcher highly familiar with each subject, which creates a citation risk when remembered wording or ideas become detached from their source. Recording everything consulted in the bibliography provides an audit trail and a defense against accidental plagiarism.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke defines relevant, well-supported, viable case studies and warns researchers to record every source as their familiarity deepens.

segments.title: Single-case and comparative case-study designs
segments.summary: A Jubilee Line dissertation shows how one large case can sustain a project when backed by more than 5,500 survey responses and about fifteen to twenty interviews, while smaller cases can be arranged for comparison.
segments.body: The single-case example examines construction of the Jubilee Line and its effects on residents above the London Underground works. The project combined a literature study with more than 5,500 survey responses and about fifteen to twenty interviews, making one infrastructure programme large enough to sustain the whole dissertation. Multiple-case designs work differently by comparing several bridges, retailers, therapies, games, or other bounded subjects. Comparison can reveal differences that a solitary case would leave invisible. The number of cases should match the scale and purpose of the available evidence.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts a survey- and interview-rich Jubilee Line dissertation with comparative multi-case designs.

segments.title: Focused laboratory work and experimental landslides
segments.summary: A brief engineering example contrasts non-laboratory methods with focused experiments that use simulations or purpose-built landslide tests when facilities are available.
segments.body: Some engineering questions still call for focused laboratory work when suitable facilities are available. The lecture contrasts simulations and physical experiments with the literature, interview, survey, and case-study methods used elsewhere in the lesson. Dr Karen Clark's landslide research provides the example: prepared mounds of earth or other material are released as experimental landslides. The setup can occupy a large part of a laboratory, making access a practical constraint. The contrast explains why most of the lesson concentrates on methods students can use when laboratories are unavailable.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts simulation and focused laboratory work with the non-laboratory scenarios, using Dr Karen Clark's experimental landslide research as the example.

segments.title: Historical context and integrated case-study evidence
segments.summary: Historical case studies need enough chronological context to judge what matters. Their chapters should then integrate interviews or survey results with literature instead of isolating each method in a separate block.
segments.body: A rough rule in the lesson is to examine as much as a hundred years on either side of a historical subject before deciding which developments matter. Much of that surrounding material may never appear in the final text, but it helps the researcher avoid treating the case in isolation. A proposed combined railway crossing and second Thames Barrier shows how bridge design, flood defenses, and transport planning can become linked research contexts. Interview or survey findings should then be woven into the relevant case-study chapters alongside the literature. This produces an integrated explanation of each case rather than separate blocks arranged only by collection method.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke discusses broad chronological context, a railway and Thames Barrier example, and integrating primary data into each case-study chapter.

segments.title: Leading questions, bias, and the interpretation of polls
segments.summary: Survey and interview questions must be fair, consistent, and neutral because leading phrasing can manufacture a preferred response, invalidate a student project, and distort the interpretation of public polling.
segments.body: Questionnaires and interviews are ethically demanding forms of public interaction. A researcher can steer an answer simply by changing the wording of a question, even when the resulting statistics look persuasive. That bias can invalidate the conclusions. The same caution applies to political and public-opinion polling because the answer may reflect the question's framing as much as the underlying circumstances. Any reported survey result should therefore be read alongside the instrument that produced it.

evidence.note: The lecture explains how leading questions introduce bias and why raw polling data must be read in light of the questions asked.

segments.title: Standardized interviews and verifiable transcripts
segments.summary: Interviewees should receive the same core questions, with follow-ups allowed, and a timed transcript should preserve who said what so the original evidence can be checked and cited.
segments.body: Using the same core questions makes interview evidence comparable across participants. Follow-up questions are still allowed when an answer needs clarification or development. A full transcript should record the speakers, wording, and timing of the exchange. Placing that record in the appendices preserves the primary evidence without consuming the main word count. The researcher can cite the interview transcript like another documentary source, allowing readers and markers to check the interpretation.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke requires consistent core interview questions and complete timed transcripts that can be placed in appendices and referenced.

segments.title: Survey deployment, privacy, and sample size
segments.summary: Online surveys can collect data while the researcher handles other commitments, but the platform must protect respondents and optional contact details must remain a deliberate choice.
segments.body: Interviews demand scheduled conversations, while an online survey can remain open for several weeks. A platform such as SurveyMonkey can collect responses while the researcher manages work or family commitments, especially when the link circulates through social media. The system should protect both researcher and respondent data, and identifying information should appear only as an optional invitation for follow-up. Larger response pools make anomalous or unserious entries easier to identify and reduce their effect on the findings.

evidence.note: The lecture compares survey and interview scheduling, discusses optional contact information and privacy, and explains the value of more responses.

segments.title: Researcher neutrality when the subject matters deeply
segments.summary: Passion for a topic cannot be allowed to override respondents’ answers: the researcher’s job is to listen, preserve what people say, and avoid inserting preferred conclusions into their evidence.
segments.body: The final warning concerns the researcher's own investment in the subject. Strong interest can sustain a project, but it can also tempt an interviewer to lead participants or replace their answers with a preferred interpretation. Academic interviews and surveys gather evidence; trying to persuade or instruct the respondent corrupts that purpose. Researchers must listen and allow participants to state their own views. Otherwise, the project loses data quality and reliability.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke warns researchers not to let passion for a topic lead respondents or put words into their mouths.
